Surah al-A'la (The Most High)

It is also called Surat Sabbih, and the majority of scholars hold that it is Meccan. Ibn al-Faras reported from some scholars that it is Medinan, because it mentions the Eid prayer and the zakat al-fitr (the charity of breaking the fast) in it. Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti rejected this with what al-Bukhari, Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: "The first of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) to come to us was Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, and they began teaching us the Qur'an. Then 'Ammar, Bilal and Sa'd came, then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) came with twenty men. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) came, and I have never seen the people of Medina rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at him, peace be upon him, until I saw the young girls and boys saying: 'This is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he has come.' He, peace be upon him, had not arrived before I had recited: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and similar surahs."

Moreover, the mention of the Eid prayer and zakat al-fitr in it is not accepted, and even if it were granted, there is no proof in it for that, as its detail will come, God willing. It has nineteen verses without any disagreement. The link between it and what precedes it is that Surat al-Tariq mentioned the creation of man and alluded to the creation of plants with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the earth that splits open﴾. Both are mentioned here in His saying: ﴿who created and proportioned﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿who brings forth the pasture﴾, ﴿then makes it dark stubble﴾. The story of plants here is clearer and more extensive, just as the story of the creation of man is there. Yes, what is in this surah is more general in that it includes man and all other created beings. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to love it.

Imam Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to love this surah: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾."

A hadith narrated by Abu 'Ubayd from Abu Tamim states that he, peace be upon him, named it "the best of the glorifying surahs."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'A'ishah who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the Witr prayer, in the first rak'ah: ﴿Glorify﴾, in the second: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and in the third: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ and the two refuges (al-Mu'awwidhatayn)." In a hadith narrated by those mentioned and others, except al-Tirmidhi, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, something similar is related, except that it does not include the two refuges.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite on the two Eids and on Friday: "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" and "Has the news of the Overwhelming come to you?" And if the Eid coincided with Friday, he would recite both of them.

al-Tabarani narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Harith who said: "The last prayer the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed was Maghrib, and in the first rak'ah he recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, and in the second: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾: that is, declare His names, may He be exalted and glorified, free from what is unfitting. So do not interpret any of the names that have come from Him as a name without a reason, nor leave it on its apparent meaning when what it is coined for is not befitting to Him, Exalted is He; and do not apply it to anyone other than Him, Glorified is He, at all when it is specific (like the Name of Majesty), or in a manner that suggests that He, Exalted, and others are equal in it. For a name that is not specific, do not say, for example, to one who has given you something: "This is my provider" in a manner that suggests that. Protect it from being cheapened, and from pronouncing it in a place unfitting for it, such as the toilet and the state of relieving oneself, and from mentioning it without the utmost humility and reverence. It may also be counted among what is unfitting to mention before one who dislikes hearing it, without necessity.

It is related from Imam Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he did not have something to give the beggar, he would say: "I have nothing to give you, or come to me at another time," or something similar, and he would not say what people say, such as: "May Allah provide for you," or "May Allah send you," or "May Allah give you," or similar. When he was asked about this, he said: "The beggar's most burdensome thing to hear and most hateful to him is the words of the one asked, which bring him nothing but refusal and deprivation. So I honour the Name of Allah, Glorified is He, from mentioning it to one who dislikes hearing it, even within a sentence." This is, may Allah be pleased with him, an extreme of piety (wara').

What has been mentioned as the explanation is based on the apparent meaning, that the word "ism" (name) is not superfluous. Many have held that it is superfluous, and it may be superfluous for a kind of glorification by way of metonymy (kinaya). Among this is the verse of Labid:

"Until the year ends, then the greeting of peace be upon you both."

So the meaning is: declare your Lord free from the attributes that are not befitting to Him. This is supported by what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and others narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: "When the verse ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: 'Put it in your bowing.' When ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said: 'Put it in your prostration.'"

It is known that what is placed in them is "Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great" and "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." And by what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, would say: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

Abd ibn Humayd and a group narrated that Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) recited that and said, "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," while he was in prayer. He was asked: "Are you adding to the Qur'an?" He said: "No, we were commanded with something and I did it."

In al-Kashshaf: glorifying His name, may He be exalted, means declaring Him free from the meanings that are not valid for it, which would be deviation (ilhad) in His names, such as compulsion (jabr) and anthropomorphism (tashbih), for example, and protecting it from cheapening and from mention not in the manner of humility and reverence. So, according to what has been said, the two meanings refer to the name, although in reality the first refers to Him, Mighty and Majestic. But just as it is valid to say, "Declare the Essence free from the attributes that are not valid for Him," it is also said, "Declare His names, which indicate perfection, free from what is contrary to them." The first meaning is not based on the word "ism" being superfluous, nor on the name being meant as the named, using the name that indicates the referent. Yes, some have held this here, and if it is based on the earlier reports, as in the claim of superfluity, then there is no harm. But if it is based on the assumption that glorification does not apply to the words coined for Him, Exalted is He, then it is nothing, because this assumption is false, as it is clear that glorification applies to them, as you have heard. The Imam has said: just as it is obligatory to declare His Essence and attributes, Exalted is He, free from defects, it is obligatory to declare the words coined for that free from obscenity and bad manners. From this one may know what is in expressing Him, exalted is His glory, with things like Layla and Nu'm, as some claim in the words of Ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified:

"Is it a lightning that appeared from the side of the valley shining, or did the veils lift from the face of Layla?"

And his saying:

"When Nu'm favoured me with a glance, may Su'da not be made happy, nor Jumal made beautiful."

And other of his verses. Some eminent scholars have criticized this and considered it bad manners and contrary to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾, the verse. Some have answered that this is not from coinage at all, and that understanding the Divine Presence from those words is only by way of allusion, as they said regarding understanding the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammara) from the cow, for example, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. The one who denies is not satisfied with this. The more apparent view is that the discourse in which this occurs is of the type of allegorical metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah), with no regard to comparing single words with single words. So it does not contain expressing Him, Mighty and Majestic, by Layla or the like. The use of allegorical metaphor regarding Him, Exalted is He, is not objectionable, to the extent that they have said it even regarding the basmalah, as is not hidden from one who examines their treatises on it. Yet perhaps they have something better than this.

A group said: the word "ism" here means "naming" (tasmiyah), and the meaning is: declare the naming of your Lord, by mentioning Him while you are magnifying Him, Glorified is He, and reverent in mentioning Him, Majestic is His glory. You know that this falls under glorifying the name, as already explained.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that the meaning is: pray in the name of your Lord, the Most High, just as you say: "Begin in the name of Allah, Exalted is He," with the preposition omitted. This is related by al-Bahr, but I do not think it is sound.

Isam al-Din said: it is not far-fetched that "ism" means "trace" (athar), i.e., glorify the traces of your Lord, the Most High, from deficiency; for His trace, Exalted is He, indicates Him, Glorified is He, just as the name does. So it would be a prohibition against finding fault in created beings, i.e., insofar as they are created by Him, Exalted is He, in a way that contradicts His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no disparity﴾. Its remoteness is not hidden, although among the attributes that follow there is something to lean on for it.

As for me, I say: if "glorify" means "declare free," then both matters, namely that "ism" is superfluous and that it is not superfluous, and attaching the glorification to it in the manner you have heard, are a possibility not far off. If its meaning is: say "Glory be" as is well known among them, then its being superfluous is certain, since neither earlier nor later generations are known to have said "Glory be to the name of my Lord, the Most High" or "Glory be to the name of Allah," and the reports are clear on this, and what is in them is interpreted by choosing the briefer form, which implies the other, as you see. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, as in the report of Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, from Ibn Jubayr: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

As for what has been said, that the name is the same as the named, and it is used as evidence by this verse and similar ones, it is something that is not relied upon at all. The discussion has already preceded at the beginning of the book, so return to it if you wish.

"Al-A'la" is an attribute of "al-Rabb" (the Lord), and by highness is meant domination and power, not place, since place is impossible for Him, Glorified is He. The early generation (salaf), although they did not interpret it this way, also held that spatial elevation is impossible for Him, Mighty and Majestic. It has been permitted to make it an attribute of "ism," and His highness means His exaltation above having any name share in the reality of its meaning.

The objection has been raised that if ﴿Who created﴾ and what follows is an attribute of the Lord, as is the apparent meaning, then it would entail separating the described noun from its attribute by an attribute of something else, which is impermissible. So one cannot say, "I saw the handsome, intelligent servant of Hind." And if it is an attribute of the name, the meaning is also disrupted, since a name cannot be described as creating and so forth.

[p. 104]

It is answered by choosing the second option, and there is no disruption. Either because "the name" means "the named," or because, since it is superfluous (muqhaman), ﴿the name of your Lord﴾ holds the position of "your Lord," so it is correct to describe it with what the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is described with. But there is a question about this. The acceptable answer is that ﴿Who﴾, on that assumption, is either in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative by way of praise (madh). The object of ﴿created﴾ is omitted, and for this reason it has been said that it is general, i.e., "Who created everything."

﴿and proportioned﴾ means: He made it balanced (mutasawiyan), and this is the basic meaning of the word. The intended sense is that He made its creation as His wisdom, glorified is He, requires in His essence and attributes. Among its meanings is what has been said, i.e., He made things equal in the matter of rulings and perfection, not that He, glorified is He, perfected some and not others. It has been rebutted by what the verse indicates of generality, against the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) in their claim that the servant creates his own actions. Al-Zamakhshari, although his doctrine is their doctrine, said here that it is general. Perhaps he did not intend true generality, or he intended it but in the sense: He created everything either directly or through an intermediary, and He placed that in the actions of the servants through His decree, glorified is He, and by enabling them to create them through their choice and their powers granted to them. From al-Kalbi: He created every living being and ﴿proportioned﴾ its front and eyes and legs. From al-Zajjaj: He created man and balanced his stature, and did not make him upside down like the beasts. In each of these there is a restriction that the apparent wording of the omission does not require.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 3:

﴿Who determined﴾ i.e., He made things according to specific measures in their genera, their kinds, their individuals, their attributes, their actions, and their terms.

﴿and then guided﴾ He directed each one of them to that from which it issues and which befits it, naturally or by choice, and He facilitated for it that for which it was created, by creating inclinations and inspirations, establishing proofs and sending down signs. Were you to trace the conditions of plants and animals, you would see in each of them what minds are bewildered by and what the books of transmitted reports cannot contain. As for the varieties of Allah's guidance to humankind in particular, they are far beyond that, and further and further still, by thousands of stations, and it is far-fetched that the sphere of expression and writing could encompass them, and none knows them except the Subtle, the All-Aware:

"Do you suppose that you are a small body, while within you the greatest universe is enfolded?"

It is also said: i.e., and by the One who determined the creation in the forms and shapes in which He fashioned them, and arranged for them the means of their livelihood through sustenance and provisions, then guided them to His religion and to knowledge of His oneness by manifesting the indications and clear proofs. It is also said: He determined their sustenance and guided them to seek it. And from Muqatil and al-Kalbi: He determined them as males and females, and guided the male to how he approaches the female. From Mujahid: He determined humans and beasts, and guided humans to good and evil, and beasts to their pastures. From al-Suddi: He determined the child's term in the womb as nine months or less or more, and guided it to come out of it at completion. It is also said: He determined the benefits in things and guided humans to extract them. The first mentioned is the preferable, and perhaps what is in the other sayings is by way of illustration, not restriction. (Al-Farra') claimed that the verse contains an elision, and the original is: "and guided and led astray," but this is nothing.

Al-Kisa'i recited «qadara» with lightening (takhfif), from "qudra" (power) or "taqdir" (determination).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 4–5:

﴿And He who brings forth the pasturage﴾, i.e., He causes to grow that which animals graze upon, fresh, moist, and luscious (yariffu), ﴿then makes it dark stubble (ghuthaʾan)﴾. The ghuthaʾ is what the torrent casts up on the side of the valley of grass and vegetation. Its root meaning, according to al-Majmaʿ (Majmaʿ al-Bahrayn), is a mixture of assorted kinds. The Arabs call a people who have gathered from various tribes akhilat (mixtures) and ghuthaʾ, and it is said ghuthaʾ with a shadda. Its plural is aghthaʾ, which is anomalous in that the plural of fuʿal is afʿal. Here it means the dried-up part of the vegetation; that is, after that He makes it dry ﴿ahwa (dark)﴾, from al-huwwa, which, as it is said, is blackness. al-Aʿlam said: it is a color inclining toward black. In al-Sihah, al-huwwa is brownness (sumra). So the meaning of ahwa is black or brown, and when vegetation dries it turns black or brown. Thus it is a emphasizing adjective for ghuthaʾ. Al-huwwa is also explained as intense greenness, and on this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

A lamyaʾ (dark-lipped beauty), on whose lips is a huwwa, a lasaʿ (darkness of the lips), and in her gums and in her canines is a shanab (whiteness of teeth).

This does not conflict with explaining it as blackness, because intense greenness appears at first glance like blackness. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) of pasturage; that is, He brought forth the pasturage while it was fresh, moist, and intensely green, then He made it stubble. Separating the circumstantial clause from its referent by a conjunction is not a foreign intrusion, especially since it is a state that follows the first immediately without delay. The secret of the anteriority is the emphasis on the state of dryness immediately following the state of freshness and luster, as if before its freshness and luxuriance are complete, it becomes stubble. Yet this is contrary to the apparent meaning. These attributes, as it is said, each of them includes gradualness; so in describing Him with them is the realization of the meaning of tarbiyah (nurturing), which is bringing a thing to its completion little by little.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾, explain His special guidance to His Messenger ﷺ, following on from the explanation of His general guidance, exalted is His majesty, to all His creatures. That general guidance is His guidance of the Messenger (ﷺ) to receive the revelation and to memorize the Qur'an, which is "a guidance for the worlds," and His granting success to the Messenger (ﷺ) in guiding all of humanity. The *sin* (in *sanuqri'uka*) is either for emphasis (*li-l-ta'kid*), or because what is meant is the recitation of what was revealed to him (ﷺ) at that time and what will be revealed to him afterwards. In that case it is a generous promise of the continuation of revelation within the promise of recitation. The attribution of the recitation to Him, exalted is He, is figurative (*majazi*): that is, "We will make you recite what We reveal to you now and hereafter, through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him)," for he (peace be upon him) is the intermediary in the revelation in all its modes. "So you will not forget" means you will not forget at all, owing to the strength of memory and mastery, even though you are unlettered (*ummi*), not knowing what the Book is or what reading is. This is to be a sign for you, together with the clear signs contained within what you recite, in terms of its inimitability (*i'jaz*) and in terms of its reporting of the unseen.

It is also permitted that the meaning is: "We will make you a reader by inspiring you with the ability to read," that is, in the Book, without anyone teaching you, as is the custom.

It has been narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he (peace be upon him) used to read writing but did not write.

The meaning of His words, ﴿so you will not forget﴾, may be the absolute negation of forgetfulness from him (peace be upon him), and a favour upon him (ﷺ) by which he was given the strength of memory. However, this, although it contradicts what is transmitted from the early generations (*salaf*) concerning the verse, is rejected by the consecutive particle *fa'* (of consequence).

It is also permitted that the meaning is the negation of forgetting the content: that is, "We will make you recite the Qur'an, so do not be heedless of it and thereby contradict it in your deeds." In that case it contains a promise of granting him (peace be upon him) success in adhering to the rulings it contains. But as you see, this is far-fetched. It has also been said that ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is a prohibition, and the *alif* is for the sake of observing the verse-ending (*fasila*), as in His words, ﴿and they led us astray from the way﴾. But this is objectionable, because forgetting is not within one's choice, so one is not prohibited from it, unless it is meant figuratively as abandoning its voluntary causes, or abandoning acting upon what the recited text contains. This also involves forcing an unnecessary interpretation. Moreover, its being written with a *ya'* implies that it is part of the word's structure and not for extension (*li-l-itlaq*), and the fact that the written form in the Mushaf differs is also a forced interpretation. Yes, it has been said that the *alif* of extension was written as a *ya'* to conform with other verse-endings and to conform with its original form, although the Imam al-Marzuqi explicitly stated that when extension is applied, the deleted letter is restored. It has also been said that it is a prohibition, but the *alif* was not deleted in it, since the jussive particle may not delete a weak letter, and the observance of the verse-ending made this acceptable here. But this too has its objections. The easiest approach for the student regarding the meaning of prohibition is to say: it is a statement (*khabar*) intended as a prohibition, according to one of the two interpretations mentioned above.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 7:**

﴿Except what God wills.﴾ This is an exceptive clause (istithna', "exception") of the type called mufarragh (a "discharged" exception, in which the excluded element is not stated), taken from the most general of the objects (al-mafa'il, "the objects"). The meaning is: "You will not forget at all anything of what We shall make you recite, except what God wills that you forget." It has been said: "that is, forever." Al-Hasan, Qatada and others said: "This is among what God, exalted is He, has decreed to abrogate (naskh, "abrogation"), so that its ruling and its recitation (tilawa, "recitation") are lifted." The apparent meaning is that forgetting (nisyan) is in its literal sense.

In al-Kashshaf, it is said: "That is, except what God wills, so He removes it from your memory by lifting its ruling and its recitation. The forgetting here is taken to mean the lifting of the ruling and recitation, as a metonymy (kinaya) for it, because what has had its ruling and recitation lifted is left aside and so forgotten. It is as if it were said: On the basis of intending both meanings in the metonymies: We shall make you recite the Qur'an, so you will not forget any part of it, and its ruling and recitation will not be lifted, except what God wills, so that you forget it and its ruling and recitation are lifted; or something similar to this." But I do not see any necessity to take account of that.

The bâ' in "bi-raf'in" etc. (in "by lifting") denotes causation. The intended meaning is either: to state the ordinary, remote cause for God's removing it from memory, since lifting the ruling and recitation usually, in most cases, leads to abandoning its recitation, because it is no longer practised in worship, and to its not coming to mind, because its ruling no longer remains, and this too usually, in most cases, leads to forgetting; or: to state the impelling cause that makes the removal from his memory, peace and blessings be upon him, seem unlikely, and it is like a cause that permits it. Whichever it is, there is no need to make the meaning of ﴿So you will not forget﴾ to be "so you will not abandon the recitation of any part of it and acting upon it." So reflect.

Furthermore, the fact that what God, glorified is He, wills to be forgotten is among what He has decreed does not imply that everything whose ruling and recitation have been lifted is something that God willed the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, to forget. For among that is what the scholars still memorise to this day. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Aisha, may God be pleased with her: "There was revealed: ten known sucklings, then they were abrogated by five known sucklings," and the hadith continues. That the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, forgot all of it after conveying it, and that what remained of it remained with some of those who heard it from him, peace and blessings be upon him, so that it was transmitted until it reached us, is far-fetched, though it is possible rationally.

It has also been said: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to hasten in reciting when Gabriel, peace be upon him, prompted him. So it was said: "Do not hasten; for Gabriel, peace be upon him, is commanded to recite it to you repeatedly until you memorise it, and then you will not forget it, ﴿except what God wills﴾, exalted is He, and then you will remember it after forgetting." You know that remembering after forgetting, though obligatory, is not what this context is teaching.

It has also been said: The exception carries the sense of paucity (qilla, "fewness"). This is customary in common usage. It is as if it were said: "except what is not known, because the will [of God] is unknown," and what is unknown is certainly fewer than what remains after the exception. So it is as if it were said: "You will not forget anything, except a little thing."

It has indeed come in Sahih al-Bukhari and others that "he, may God bless him and grant him peace, dropped a verse in his recitation during the prayer, and it was the Dawn Prayer. Ubayy thought it had been abrogated, so he asked him, peace and blessings be upon him, and he said: 'I forgot it.'" Then, peace and blessings be upon him, is not left in forgetting even a little; rather God reminds him or makes it easy for someone to remind him.

Thus, in al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit): "When he, may God bless him and grant him peace, heard the recitation of Abbad ibn Bishr, he said: 'Such-and-such a verse in such-and-such a surah has reminded me of such-and-such.'"

It has been said: The exception carries the sense of paucity, and by it is meant negation, figuratively, as in their saying: "Say, who says such-and-such?" It has been said: The discourse on this is like the line: "And there is no fault in them, except that their swords ..." (the verse). The meaning is: "So you will not forget, except with a forgetting that does not exist." In the Hawashi al-'Isamiyya on Anwar al-Tanzil, it is stated that the exception on this reading serves to emphasise the generality of the negation, not to break its generality. It may also be said: the exception is from the most general of times, so: "You will not forget at any time, except the time of God's will that you forget, but He, glorified is He, does not will it." This is like what has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He, about the people of Paradise: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, and we have already mentioned that. To this view al-Farra' went, and he said: "He, exalted is He, did not will that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, forget anything; however, the purpose of the exception is to show that if He, exalted is He, had wished to make him, peace and blessings be upon him, forgetful of it, He would have been able to do so, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away what We have revealed to you﴾." Then we affirm with certainty that He, exalted is He, did not will that, and He said to him, may God bless him and grant him peace: ﴿If you were to associate partners, your deeds would surely be voided﴾, though he, peace and blessings be upon him, never associated anything at all.

In sum, the benefit of this exception is that God, exalted is He, makes known His power, so that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, knows that the absence of forgetting is from God's grace and kindness, not from his own strength; that is, so that this is greatly strengthened, or so that others may know it. The fact that God does not will his forgetting, peace and blessings be upon him, is known from outside the text, and from it is the verse: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾, to the end of the verse...

Abu Hayyan has indicated what al-Farra' said and the view preceding it, and he rejected both with the utmost rejection, because he did not grasp their real meaning. He said: "It should not be in the speech of God, exalted is He, nor even in eloquent speech." That is a rash claim on his part, may God forgive him. Furthermore, the intended meaning of the negation of forgetting any part of the Qur'an is the negation of complete and continuous forgetting of what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would not be left upon. What the earlier report contains is not of this kind. The scholars have mentioned that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is not left in forgetting in matters that are fundamentals of the sharia and obligations, but he may be left in forgetting what is not among them, or among them but belongs to the etiquettes and sunnas. This has been reported from Imam al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, so let it be memorised.

The turn (iltifat) to the Sublime Name (Allah) in all the other aspects is to cultivate awe and to signal that the will revolves around the title of divinity (uluhiyya), which entails all the other attributes. The linking of the verse with what precedes it in the manner we mentioned is what he chose in al-Irshad. Abu Hayyan said: "When He, glorified is He, commanded him, may God bless him and grant him peace, to glorify (tasbih), and that could not be completed except by reciting what had been revealed to him of the Qur'an, and he, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to ponder in himself lest he forget, He, glorified is He, removed that from him by informing him that He, mighty and majestic, would make him recite, and that he would not forget except what He wills to make him forget for a benefit." There is a consideration in this that is not hidden.

If it were said that ﴿We shall make you recite﴾ is a resumptive (isti'naf) clause that stands in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the glorification or for the command to it, it would indicate the grandeur of the act of making recitation and that it is something that should be met with the glorification and exaltation of God, exalted is He, then that would be easier than what has been mentioned. Similar to it is that it stands in the position of causal explanation, in the sense of: "Prepare yourself to receive the outpouring upon you by glorifying God, exalted is He, for We: ﴿shall make you recite, so you will not forget, except what God wills﴾." That implies an indication of the excellence of glorification, and many reports have come concerning it, and al-Tha'labi mentioned some of them, and Ibn al-Shaykh related it in his glosses on the tafsir of al-Baydawi. And God, exalted is He, knows best its soundness.

﴿Indeed He knows the open and what is hidden.﴾ This is a causal explanation for what precedes it. Here "the open" (al-jahr) means what appears, whether in speech, action, or otherwise, and it is not restricted to speech, by the evidence of the contrast with "what is hidden." That is: God, exalted is He, knows what appears and what is concealed of matters, among which is your state and your eagerness to preserve all that is revealed to you. So He will make you recite what He makes you recite, and will preserve you from forgetting what He wills, and will make you forget what He wills, in consideration of the benefits and the legislative wisdoms attached to each.

It has been said: it is an emphasis (tawkid) on everything preceding it and an emphasis on what follows it. It has been said: it is an emphasis on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall make you recite﴾, and so on. On this view, "the open" means what appears of speech; that is, He, glorified is He, knows your loud recitation with Gabriel, peace be upon him, and what prompted you to it from fear of forgetting, so He knows what contains the good, of preserving and of causing to forget. Or the sense is: "So do not fear, for I will suffice you against what you fear." It has been said: it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, but this is nothing, as you see.

﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿We shall make you recite﴾, as the shift to the narrative mode (iltifāt ilā al-ḥikāya) indicates. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) that is relevant to what you have heard. The attaching of ease (taysīr) to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, although the common usage is to attach it to matters that are made easy for the agent, as in His words ﴿and ease my task for me﴾, serves to signal the great firmness of his establishment in ease and his disposal of it, to the point that it became a firmly rooted disposition (malaka rāsikha) for him, as though he, peace be upon him, had been created upon it. That is: We will grant you continuous success (tawfīq mustamirr) in the easy way in every chapter of the religion, in knowledge and in teaching, in guidance and in being guided. Thus included in this is the ease of receiving both channels of revelation, and comprehending what they contain of the rulings of the tolerant Sharia and the divine laws, of what pertains to the perfection of his noble self, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the perfection of others, as the subsequent fāʾ (the particle "then") makes clear. So says al-Irshād (Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm, the tafsir of Abū al-Suʿūd).

It has been said: the intended meaning of "the easy way" is the path that is easiest and simplest for preserving the revelation. It has also been said: it is the easy, upright Sharia. And it has been said: it refers to good matters in the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, such as victory, elevated status, and high rank in Paradise. Some matters of the religion have been added to these. With this addition it is a good and general interpretation, and a matter also appears to be dominant in it.

The fa' in His words ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾ means: so remind the people in the manner We have facilitated for you, with what is revealed to you, and guide them to what it contains of the legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyyah), as you used to do. It was also said: the fa' means: remind after the matter has become settled (istatabba), that is, has become straight and prepared for you. If it means: persist in reminding after the matter has become straight for you, through your recitation of the Revelation and your teaching of the Qur'an, such that you forget from it only what the interest requires you to forget, and your facilitating of the easy path (al-tariqah al-yusra) in every chapter of the religion, then that is so. Otherwise, it is nothing.

The restriction of the reminding to the benefit of the reminder is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had already reminded and exerted himself greatly in it. He left no bowstring unstrung (lam yada fi al-qaws manza'an), he took every path and left no narrow or broad way unexplored, out of eagerness for faith and for the Tawhid of the King, the Judge. Yet this only increased some people in disbelief, obstinacy, rebellion and corruption. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him (ﷺ) with lightening upon him, since his eagerness for their faith was about to direct the arrows of destruction towards him, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this message﴾. The meaning is that he should confine the reminding to those in whom benefit is generally hoped for, whether all of them or some of them, those from whom reminding may be expected, and that he should not weary his noble self in reminding those whom reminding only increases in haughtiness, aversion, corruption and delusion, from among those whose hearts are sealed, as in His words: ﴿So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, and His words, glorified is He: ﴿So turn away from whoever turns away from Our remembrance﴾. He (ﷺ) was taught about the one whose heart was sealed by Allah, exalted is He, informing him of it, peace be upon him. So after the conveying and the establishing of the proof, he (ﷺ) is not obliged to repeat the reminding to one who is known to have a sealed heart.

Page 108

Accordingly, the condition here is on its literal sense. It was also said that it is not so; rather, it expresses the improbability of benefit with respect to those mentioned, as a reproach against them for their obstinacy, as if it were said: do what you are commanded to do so that you may be rewarded, even if they do not benefit from it. In this there is consolation for him (ﷺ). The first view is preferred, because it keeps the condition on its literal sense, and because it is more fitting with His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 10:

﴿Soon will be mindful whoever fears﴾. That is: soon will be mindful, through your reminding, whoever is of such a disposition that he fears Allah, exalted is He, with the true fear due to Him; or whoever fears Allah, exalted is He, in general, so that this increases through the reminder, and he reflects upon the matter of what you remind him of, comes to know its reality, and thus believes in it. It has also been said that "in" (in) here means "when" (idh), as in the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And you will be superior if you are believers﴾, meaning: since you are believers; because He, glorified is He, did not inform them that they would be superior except after their faith. And [it is also like] the words of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, at the visiting of the graves: "And we, if Allah wills, will surely join you."

The Kufians affirmed this meaning for it, citing what has been mentioned and its parallels, while those who deny it answered these arguments with what is in al-Mughni and elsewhere. It has also been said that it means "qad" (indeed), and Qutrub held this meaning. 'Isam al-Din said: The intended meaning is that reminding should be with what is important to the one being reminded. So it is fitting to remind the disbelievers of faith, not of the branches (of religion) such as prayer, fasting and pilgrimage, since these do not benefit him without faith; and to remind a believer who neglects prayer of it, rather than of faith, for example; and so on. It is as if it were said: remind each one with what benefits him and suits him. Al-Farra', al-Nahhas, al-Jurjani and al-Zahrawi said: the speech is elliptical, and the original is: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾, and if it does not benefit, as in the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾. The apparent point is that those who do not hold to the concept of implication by opposition (mafhum al-mukhalafa), whether it is the implication of a condition or otherwise, will not find this verse problematic, as is not hidden.

ويَتَجَنَّبُها (wa-yatajannabuhā): that is, he avoids the Reminder and keeps far from it, ﴿al-ashqā﴾ (the most wretched), who is the disbeliever who persists in denying the Return and similar matters, firmly asserting the negation of that, in a manner that would call for fear; and he is the most wretched of the types of disbelievers. It has been said: the intended meaning is the disbeliever who goes to excess in enmity toward the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa. It has been narrated that the verse was revealed concerning them both, for he is more wretched than one who does not go to excess. It has been said: the intended meaning is the disbeliever in general, for he is more wretched than the wrongdoer (al-fasiq). It has also been said: the one being compared is the disbelievers of all the other nations, for since the believer of this Ummah is happier than the believers of theirs, the disbeliever of this Ummah is more wretched than their disbelievers. The most correct view in my opinion regarding the meaning of al-ashqā is what has preceded.

﴿Alladhī yaṣlā al-nār al-kubrā﴾ (﴿Who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾). That is, the lowest layer among the layers of the Fire, as al-Farrā' said. There is no improbability in the Fire of the Hereafter having degrees, with some of it greater than others and more intense in heat.

al-Ḥasan said: "al-Kubrā" is the Fire of the Hereafter, and "al-Ṣughrā" is the Fire of this world. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Your fire is one part of seventy parts of the Fire of Jahannam."

In a narration of Imam Aḥmad on his authority, also traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed this fire is one part of a hundred parts of Jahannam."

Perhaps the number seventy is used to denote abundance, and it is frequently so used.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 13:

﴿Then he will neither die therein﴾ and thus find rest, ﴿nor live﴾, meaning a life that benefits him. It has also been said that the soul of one of them will lodge in his throat, so that it neither leaves him to die nor returns to its place in the body to live. This view is in need of qualification by something like "a complete life," and it is still not free from scrutiny. Thumma (then) here indicates a gradation in rank, for this state is more terrible and greater than the Great Fire itself.

ʿIṣām al-Dīn said: It is possible that this statement is a metaphor (kināya) for the absence of salvation, because salvation from punishment comes only through works performed in an abode where the worker dies and lives, and the wording is closer to this meaning. How so? Whereas what fits the previous meaning would be: "then he will not be dead therein nor alive," so reflect. End of quotation.

Whether what he mentions fits the previous meaning better than what is in the sublime wording is an evident objection. The apparent view is that the wording fits it, along with its inclusion of the observance of the rhyme (fawāṣil). Likewise, the justification for taking what was mentioned as a metaphor for the absence of salvation is obscure, and perhaps for this reason he ordered reflection. It may be said that a statement like this is said of one who falls into hardship and remains in it, so it is not far-fetched that it contains an allusion to their eternal abiding in punishment. The matter of the gradational thumma is also evident on this reading, since it is clear that abiding eternally in the Great Fire is more terrible than entering it and burning in it.

Know that the non-death in the Fire, as stated by more than one scholar, is specific to the disbelievers. As for the sinning believers who enter it,
page 109
they will die therein. This is supported by what Muslim transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "As for the people of the Fire who are its people, they will neither die therein nor live. But there are people whom the Fire will touch because of their sins — or he said, their misdeeds — and Allah will cause them to die a death, until when they become charcoal, He will permit intercession, and they will be brought in clusters and scattered on the rivers of Paradise. Then it will be said: O people of Paradise, pour water over them, and they will sprout like a seed in the flood debris."

Al-Hafiz Ibn Rajab said: It indicates that these people truly die and their souls depart from their bodies. This is reinforced by the emphatic verbal noun in the Prophet's (ﷺ) words, "Allah caused them to die a death."

Clearer than this is what al-Bazzar transmitted from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The least in portion among the people of Paradise are a people whom Allah will bring out of the Fire, and the Lord, blessed and exalted, will be pleased with them. That is because they did not associate anything with Allah, so they will be cast out onto the wasteland and will sprout as grass sprouts, until the spirits enter their bodies. Then they will say: Our Lord, as You brought us out of the Fire and returned the spirits to our bodies, turn our faces away from the Fire. So He will turn their faces away from the Fire."

This death, according to what more than one scholar has chosen, comes after they taste the punishment they deserve in proportion to their sins, as Muslim's hadith suggests. Their remaining in it dead until intercession is permitted, since it necessitates the delay of their entry into Paradise for that period, constitutes a completion of their punishment in another form. Thus their sins have required that they be punished with the Fire for a period, then be detained therein without punishment for a period. They are like one who committed a sin in this world, was beaten, and was then imprisoned after the beating as a recompense for his sin. They do not remain alive therein without punishment, like its guardians, either so that the sight of it will be more distant from terrifying them, or so that death and the departure of the spirit are also part of the completion of the punishment.

Al-Qurtubi said: It is possible that their death occurs at the moment of their entry into it, and that their entry and the withholding of Paradise's bliss from them during their stay in it is a punishment for them, like confinement in prison without shackles or chains, for example. It is also possible that they are in pain at the moment of their death, similar to the pain of the disbeliever after his death and before the Hour, and that this is lighter than their pain if they had remained alive, just as the disbeliever's pain in his grave after death is lighter than his pain when he is cast into the Fire after resurrection. And this, as you see, is weak.

In Matami al-Afham: It is possible that by the death mentioned, and in the hadith, what is meant is sleep, for Allah the Exalted called sleep a "death" (wafāh), since there is in it a kind of absence of sensation.

In a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "When Allah the Exalted causes the monotheists to enter the Fire, He causes them to die therein. Then when He, glorified is He, wishes them to come out, the punishment will touch them at that very hour." End of quotation.

What is relied upon is what we mentioned first. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 14:

﴿Indeed, he has succeeded﴾, i.e., he was saved from what is disliked and attained what he hoped for. ﴿who purifies himself﴾, i.e., he purified himself from shirk (associating partners with God) by remembering and taking admonition from the reminder. This interpretation is related from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said regarding this: "Whoever bears witness that there is no god but Allah, renounces the rivals (al-andad), and bears witness that I am the Messenger of Allah."

Some scholars considered two meanings together and said: i.e., he purified himself from disbelief and disobedience. Accordingly, what was mentioned earlier may be an instance of limiting the statement to the most important matter. It was also said: "tazakka" means he increased in piety and fear of God, from "zaka'" (growth), which is increase. It was said: he purified himself for the prayer. It was said: he paid the zakat, and this was related from Abu al-Ahwas, Qatadah, and a group of others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 15:

﴿And he remembers the name of his Lord﴾ with his tongue and his heart, not with his tongue alone while his heart is heedless; for such remembrance carries no reward, and so it should not be included in that which brings about success (falah). Remembrance of the heart (al-dhikr al-qalbi) by calling His name, exalted is He, to mind in the heart, although it is undoubtedly praiseworthy, yet to intend it specifically by what is mentioned is contrary to the apparent meaning, and al-Tabarsi (Majma' al-Bayan) related this from some scholars. As for what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding his saying, namely: he remembered his return (ma'ad) and his standing before his Lord, mighty and majestic, it is evident in it, and in the insertion of the word "name" (ism). Some of the Hanafis held that by this remembrance is meant the opening takbir (takbirat al-iftitah), as if it were said: "And glorify (kabbir) for the opening."

﴿And prayed﴾: that is, the five daily prayers, as Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was also related in a marfu' hadith. It was said: the obligatory prayer and whatever of the supererogatory prayers is possible. By this it was argued for the obligation of the takbir, since success was tied to it and it fell between two obligations, indeed two obligatory duties: purification from shirk and prayer. Moreover, caution in acts of worship is obligatory, so the mere possibility (of error) does no harm. Also, the opening (of prayer) is permissible with any of His names, mighty and majestic, which is evident. And (it is argued) that the takbir is a condition and not a pillar, because of the conjunction with "fa" (then), and the conjunction of the whole upon a part is like the conjunction of the general upon the specific; and even if it is permissible, it does not occur with it. Moreover, even if its soundness were granted with effort, there must be a reason (nukta) for claiming its occurrence in the miraculous speech, and where it does not appear, its claim is not valid, nor is the building of the pillarhood upon it. The truth is that, with what you have heard, this is an argument that is not strong. It was also said: it refers specifically to "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" before the prayer, but this is nothing.

And from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "purified himself" (tazakka) means he gave the charity of fitr (sadaqat al-fitr); "and remembered the name of his Lord" means he glorified (kabbara) on the day of Eid.

﴿And prayed﴾: the Eid prayer.

And from a group of the early generation (salaf) there is what its apparent meaning implies, and it has been objected that the prayer is mentioned before zakat in the Qur'an, and that the surah is Meccan, and at that time there was no Eid nor fitr. It was answered that this applies when they are mentioned by name; but when they are mentioned by verb, their precedence is not consistent, and from it is: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾. Moreover, it is possible that the departure from the usual order here is to guide to the fact that this zakat, which is mentioned first in speech, should be given precedence in action over the prayer, and for this reason they used to give it out before praying the Eid, as came in the reports. As for the surah being Meccan, it is not agreed upon; and on the view of its being Meccan, which is the more correct, this would be among what had its ruling delayed after its revelation. And I say: it may be said that "purified himself" means he cleansed himself from shirk by believing in his heart, "and remembered the name of his Lord" means he said: there is no god but Allah, "and prayed" means the obligatory prayer.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas what supports this, so that "purified himself" indicates affirmation by the heart (al-tasdiq bil-janan), "and remembered the name of his Lord" indicates utterance by the tongue, and "and prayed" indicates action by the limbs, since prayer is the pillar of religion and the best of the bodily acts, and it forbids indecency and wrongdoing; so it is no wonder that it is mentioned, and all bodily acts and heart-directed acts of worship are intended. It may also be said: he confined himself to mentioning prayer because the obligatory and required bodily duties were not complete on the day this surah was revealed, and prayer was the most important thing revealed, if anything else had been revealed. 'Ata related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Yazid al-Nahwi from Ikrimah and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, that the first of the Qur'an revealed in Mecca was: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, then "Nun", then al-Muzzammil, then al-Muddaththir, then "Tabbat", then ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾, then ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾. Then indeed, following "There is no god but Allah" is "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (ﷺ), and the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, that was sought is the totality of the two sentences; so there is no distance in intending by His remembrance in the verse (the whole), and if the mention of His name, mighty and majestic, in the second sentence is considered in the way in which it came as a remembrance of Him, exalted is He, the matter of intention becomes nearer; and this view is not without merit.

The word "qad" (indeed/certainly): because when the report is given of the bad condition of one who turns away from the remembrance in the Hereafter, the listener expects a report of the good condition of the one who remembers in it. It is not far-fetched that the sentence is a resumed (mustaʼnafa) sentence, answering a question that arose from the explanation of the condition of the one who turns away and the silence regarding the condition of the one who remembers, who fears; as if it were said: what is the condition of him who remembers? So it was said: ﴿He has indeed succeeded﴾ to the end. The apparent wording would have been: "He has indeed succeeded, he who remembers," but he placed "he who purified himself" to the end in the position of "he who remembers," as an indication of explaining the one who remembers by his characteristics.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, you prefer the present life﴾ is a turning away (idrab, a shift of discourse) from an implied matter to which the speech leads, as if it were said: after the explanation of what leads to success, you do not do that, ﴿nay, you prefer﴾ etc. Perhaps this is what was meant by the one who said: it is a turning away from ﴿He has succeeded﴾ etc. It was also said: it is a turning away from explaining the state of the one who remembers and the one who avoids, to explaining that this explanation and its like does not benefit the rebellious, in a manner that includes the explanation of the cause of non-benefit, which is preferring the life of this world. The address, on this view, is to the disbelieving wretched ones of Makkah. On the first view, it may be addressed to them too; the meaning of preferring the life of this world is then contentment with it and being at rest in it, and turning away from the Hereafter entirely, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, and are content with the life of this world and at rest with it﴾, the verse. It may also be addressed to all people by way of predominance (taghlib), so that the meaning of preferring it is more general than what has been mentioned, namely the inclination, which people generally do not escape, to favour the side of this world over the Hereafter in striving and in ordering the means.

And there is, from Ibn Mas'ud, what implies this. The shift to the second person (iltifat) on the first view is for intensifying the rebuke, and on the second view likewise regarding the disbelievers, and for intensifying the reproach regarding the Muslims. It was also said: there is no iltifat, because it is by the implied (taqdir) "say" (qul). ʿAbd Allah, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu ʿAmr, al-Zaʿfarani and Ibn Muqsim read: «yu'thirun» with the yaʾ of the third person.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the subject of "you prefer" (tu'thirun), serving to reinforce the rebuke and reproach. That is: you prefer it over the Hereafter, while the reality is that the Hereafter is better in itself, because its bliss, although it is at the utmost degree of pleasure, is pure, free from any admixture of harm, and everlasting, with no cessation to it. The non-mention of explaining how the bliss of this world is clouded by troubles and cut off after a short while is due to its being extremely evident.

ـ

**﴿Indeed, this﴾** is a reference to what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, namely to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾. This is also reported from Qatadah. Others, and more than one, have said: it refers to what was mentioned of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾, and so on. God willing, there will come in a hadith (later) what bears witness to it. Al-Dahhak said: it refers to the Qur'an, so the verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is in the Scriptures of the former peoples﴾. And from Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Suddi: it refers to what all the surahs contain together, but this is far-fetched.

**﴿In the former scriptures﴾**, meaning: it is established in them, its meaning. Al-A'mash, Harun and Ismah, both of them from Abu 'Amr, read the letter ḥāʾ (in ﴿الصُّحُفِ﴾) with sukūn (ṣuḥuf → ṣuḥf), and likewise in what follows. This is the dialect of Tamim, according to al-Lawami'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 87, verse 19:

﴿The scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿the former scrolls﴾. Its indefiniteness, its description as being ancient, and then its clarification and explanation are, in magnifying its status, nothing that is hidden. The scrolls of Abraham were ten, and likewise the scrolls of Moses, peace be upon him; and what is meant by them is other than the Torah.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated, on the authority of Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how many books did Allah the Exalted send down?' He said: 'One hundred and four books. He sent down fifty scrolls to Shith, thirty scrolls to Idris, ten scrolls to Abraham, and ten scrolls to Moses before the Torah, and He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what were the scrolls of Abraham?' He said: 'They were all parables: O king, dominated by the afflicted and deceived, I did not send you to gather the world, part of it upon part of it, but I sent you to turn away from Me the supplication of the oppressed, for I do not turn it back even if it comes from a disbeliever. And it is incumbent upon the intelligent person, so long as he is not overcome in his intellect, to have three hours: an hour in which he communes with his Lord, an hour in which he takes account of his soul and reflects upon what he has done, and an hour in which he is alone for his needs from the lawful; for in this hour there is help for those hours, a gathering and an easing of the hearts. And it is incumbent upon the intelligent person to be perceptive of his time, attentive to his affairs, and guarding his tongue, for whoever counts his speech as part of his deeds speaks little except concerning what concerns him. And it is incumbent upon the intelligent person to seek three things: provision for livelihood, provision for the Hereafter, or enjoyment in what is not forbidden.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what were the scrolls of Moses?' He said: 'They were all lessons: I wonder at one who is certain of death and yet rejoices; at one who is certain of the Fire and yet laughs; at one who sees the world and its turning over its people and yet is at peace with it; at one who is certain of destiny and yet becomes angry; and at one who is certain of the Reckoning and yet does not act.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, has anything been sent down to you of what was in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses?' He said: 'O Abu Dharr, yes: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself﴾ ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ ﴿But you prefer the worldly life﴾ ﴿while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾.'"

And Allah the Exalted knows best the soundness of the hadith.

Abu Raja' read "Ibrahama" (إبْرَهَمَ) with the alif and the ya' omitted and the ha' vowelled with a fatha or a kasra, while Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra read it only with a kasra. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn al-Zubayr read "Ibrahaam" (إبْراهامَ) with two alifs throughout the Qur'an. Malik ibn Dinar read "Ibraham" (إبْراهَمَ) with an alif, a fatha on the ha', and without a ya'. And there came, as Ibn Khalawayh said, "Ibrahum" (إبْرَهُمَ) with a damma on the ha', without an alif or a ya'. This is one of the Arabs' treatments of non-Arabic names, for Ibrahim, according to the correct view, is of that kind. Al-Kirmani, in his 'Aja'ib, related that it is an Arabic name derived from al-burhama, which is intensity of gaze; and its lineage has already been mentioned, and likewise the lineage of Moses, may Allah the Exalted bless both of them and grant them peace.
